# Your Retail Dictionary: Industry Terms Every Retailer Should Know

Knowing and understanding retail terminology is essential for everyone working in the industry, from retail store owners to wholesale suppliers and everyone in between. Especially if you’ve just started your career in retail, it can be challenging to keep up with the jargon you might hear every day.


That’s why we’ve put together this detailed retail glossary that explains key retail industry terms in simple language. Whether you’re new to the field or just looking to brush up on your knowledge, this retail dictionary with comprehensive retail definitions will help you navigate the retail lingo confidently.


#### Optimize your retail operations and grow faster


From intuitive POS and stock management features to AI-driven reporting, Lightspeed gives you all the tools you need to run your retail business smarter and grow faster.

## **Retail operations and store management terms**


### **Anchor store**


An anchor store is a big department store in a mall. Depending on the size of a shopping center, there can be more than one, generally at either end of the building. Their wide range of merchandise and massive advertising budgets help attract customers to the mall. Those shoppers often spend money at the anchor stores as well as at the surrounding smaller retailers. This role is usually filled by large, well-known chain retailers such as Macy’s.


### **Big box store**


A big box store is a store that provides a wide variety of products in a large physical space. These stores focus on large sales volumes, allowing a lower[profit margin](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/retail-profit-margins/) for items and competitive prices for customers. The stores are usually very minimalist in design. Walmart, Ikea and Home Depot are examples of big box stores.


### **Brick and click**


A brick-and-click business is a retail store with a brick-and-mortar establishment, as well as an ecommerce website. In modern business, it’s widely accepted that to achieve the highest lead conversion rate for your business you should have a physical presence instead of being based solely online. A store that has a traditional outlet and the opportunity to shop online will enjoy more profit. The brick and click aspects of a business ensure that customers from all around the world have access to your product or service.


### **Cashwrap**


The cashwrap is the main checkout area of your retail store, where customers pay for their items. It’s also known as the point of sale or the point of purchase. A cashwrap is sometimes staffed by sales personnel trained to upsell customers, getting them to add anything from extended warranties, gift wrapping or participation in a store loyalty card program to their purchase. The approach to a cashwrap will frequently be flanked by shelves stocked with items picked and priced to entice customers into making an impulse buy on their way out.


### **Cooperative**


A cooperative is a business that’s owned by a community of members rather than by investors or corporate shareholders. They range from huge, multibillion businesses to tiny community enterprises. Cooperatives are present in many industries across the country, from housing to health care, and retail to social care.


### **Electronic article surveillance**


Electronic article surveillance, often abbreviated to EAS, is a technological method for preventing shoplifting. Tags and labels are affixed to high-value or frequently stolen goods and then are removed or deactivated by staff after being purchased so that they don’t set off the alarm system. At the exits of the store, a detection system sounds an alarm to alert the staff when it senses active tags are passing through.


### **Footfall**


[Footfall](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/retail-store-foot-traffic/) is the measurement of the number of people entering your business premises. By counting how many people enter your retail space, other important key metrics can be calculated, such as conversion rates and your average transaction value (ATV).


### **Franchise**


Some businesses expand by distributing their products via a licensing relationship. A[franchisor](https://www.franchise.org/faqs/basics/what-is-a-franchise) issues a license to the franchisee to operate under the business’ name. In most circumstances, the franchisor will specify the products and services to be provided to customers by the franchisee, provide an operating system and operational support. Subway and McDonald’s are some of the most popular businesses that operate through franchising systems.


### **High speed retail**


High speed retail is all about optimizing the customer’s shopping experience and ensuring that it goes as quickly and smoothly as possible. Popular examples of high speed retail are drive-through grocery stores, mobile businesses such as food trucks or any business that utilizes an urgent promotion or limited-time sales.


### **Mystery shopping**


Mystery shopping is a research method that’s used to gather feedback. While the most common means of conducting this research is in person, it can also be conducted over the phone or by making online inquiries, depending on the kind of feedback required. Though mystery shopping is commonly used for market research, it’s also used to gather data about other factors that would impact a customer’s experience. For example, friendliness of staff or quality of food in a restaurant.


### **Niche retailing**


A niche retailer only sells a single type of product within a specific category. While[niche retailers](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/niche-markets-are-ecommerce-winners/) generally don’t appeal to large groups of consumers, they can meet the specific needs of the small groups that they target. Niche retail trends don’t correlate with trends in large, general retailers that sell a variety of goods and as such try to reach as many customers as possible.


### **Off-price retailers**


Off-price retailers are retailers who provide high-quality items at extremely cheap prices. They usually sell second-hand goods or items that are out of season. These retailers offer brand name soft goods at low prices. They can afford to do this by purchasing irregular pieces straight from the manufacturer, canceled orders, goods purchased by other retailers and end-of-season clearance items.


### **Self-checkout**


Self-checkout is a terminal installed in a retail store that lets customers scan and pay for their purchases independently, without needing a cashier. A store employee is usually still available at self-checkout terminals to assist shoppers if needed or resolve issues. Retailers use self-checkout to reduce checkout queues during busy periods and decrease labor costs.


### **Shrinkage**


Shrinkage is the loss of goods that can be chalked up to reasons such as theft by employees, shoplifting, admin errors, vendor fraud, damage in store or in transit and cashier errors.[Inventory shrinkage](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/inventory-shrinkage-what-it-is-and-how-to-prevent-it/) is the difference between recorded inventory and actual inventory. The resulting loss of money is a huge problem for retailers.


## **Inventory and supply chain terms**


### **ABC inventory analysis**


[ABC inventory analysis](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/abc-inventory-analysis/) is an inventory management method that groups products based on their value and importance to a business. **A-items** are a small number of products that generate most of the revenue, **B-items** are moderately valuable, while **C-items** are lower-value products. ABC inventory analysis helps retailers make better decisions around purchasing, stocking and replenishment.


### **Bulk**


Bulk is buying goods in large quantities. A retailer buys wholesale products in bulk and marks them up to sell to customers.


### **Consignment merchandise**


Consignment merchandise or[consignment inventory](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-is-consignment-inventory/) is the inventory that isn’t owned or paid for by the retailer until it’s sold. Consignment is a business deal whereby the retailer agrees to pay a seller for goods after they have sold.


Businesses that operate on consignment are usually retail stores that specialize in a specific type of consumer product. The business takes items from the seller and agrees to pay a percentage of the funds generated if the goods are sold.


### **Consumer packaged goods**


Consumer packaged goods, often abbreviated to CPG, are items that are used daily by the average consumer. Goods in this category are ones that don’t have a long shelf life and need to be replaced frequently, compared to goods that are usable for prolonged periods of time.


The CPG market will always have consumers, but it’s competitive due to high market saturation and extremely low consumer switching costs. The most obvious examples of a CPG are consumables such as food, beverages, tobacco, clothing and household products.


### **Cycle counting**


[Cycle counting](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/cycle-counting/) (also known as a partial stocktake) is the practice of counting selected inventory on an ongoing basis, instead of counting every product at once. Retailers typically do it daily, weekly or monthly. Cycle counting is one of the most efficient inventory counting methods for retailers. It allows them to maintain accurate inventory levels and spot errors without needing to shut down store operations or work extra hours.


### **Dead stock**


[Dead stock](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/dead-stock/) is inventory that has little or no realistic chance of selling at its original price, often because it is obsolete, damaged, out of season or no longer in demand. This problem often results from overordering, shifting consumer tastes or poor seasonal planning.


Because dead stock ties up shelf space and working capital, retailers usually try to address it quickly. Some ways to manage dead stock include bundling it with popular items, heavily discounting it, liquidating it to third-party resellers or writing it off as a donation.


### **Demand forecasting**


[Demand forecasting](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/demand-forecasting-methods/) is the process of estimating how much customers are likely to buy in a future period based on historical data, market tends and other influencing factors. Accurate demand forecasting helps retailers ensure the right products are available at the right time and minimize the risks of stockouts or overstocking. It also enables retailers to staff store floors appropriately during seasonal peaks.


### **Dropshipping**


Dropshipping is a business model that allows a company to operate in a very simplistic manner. This kind of business doesn’t need to maintain inventory on-hand, own a warehouse to store products, or worry about shipping them to customers directly. A retailer partners with a dropship supplier who takes care of virtually the entire process for them. Once the product is ordered, the dropship supplier will ship them directly to the retailer’s customer.


### **Economic order quantity (EOQ)**


Economic order quantity (EOQ) is a method used to determine the ideal order size a retailer should purchase to minimize total inventory expenses (ordering costs and inventory holding costs, in particular). A retailer may use EOQ as a starting point when replenishing a stable product. It works best when demand and costs are steady, but it loses accuracy when things fluctuate.


### **FIFO (First In, First Out)**


[FIFO](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-is-fifo/) (First In, First Out) is an inventory management method where the oldest purchased goods are sold before newer stock. FIFO helps prevent inventory from becoming outdated, reduce waste and ensure compliance with products that have expiration dates. This is particularly useful for businesses selling food and cosmetics.


### **Forecast**


An estimate of the future demand for goods or services. Demand in the past is used to calculate future demand, with adjustments for trends and seasonal trends.


### **Fulfillment center**


A fulfillment center is a facility where online orders are received, stored, picked, packed and shipped to customers. Fulfillment centers help retailers ship orders faster, save money on delivery and handle busy seasons without needing their own warehouses. On the downside, they charge expensive storage fees and limit how retailers can customize their packaging.


### **Integrated supply chain**


Integrated supply chain management refers to a specific resource planning approach to traditional supply chain management. Rather than having multiple systems within the organization, a business manages and facilitates relationships with all of its suppliers and distributors through a centralized system.


### **Inventory management**


Inventory management is important for businesses of any size. It is crucial for knowing when to restock items, what amounts to purchase or produce, and what price to pay to suppliers. Small businesses can automate day-to-day stock management by adopting POS technology and basic[inventory management techniques](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/inventory-management-techniques/) .


### **Inventory reconciliation**


[Inventory reconciliation](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/inventory-reconciliation/) means the process of matching inventory levels in your POS system with the stock physically on hand in your stores and stockroom. Discrepancies may happen from data entry errors, vendor miscounts, unrecorded sales or returns, damage or bigger issues like employee theft or supplier fraud.


Tools like[Lightspeed Scanner](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/scanner/) can help retailers speed up inventory reconciliation by scanning barcodes and updating stock counts instantly in your POS without manual paperwork.


### **Inventory turnover**


The average amount of times that inventory that is in stock is sold or used during a given period is known as[inventory turnover](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/inventory-turnover-ratio/) . In most circumstances, high stock turnover is good, as it’s a sign that you’re selling a lot without overstocking. If a business wishes to calculate it, the cost of goods sold must be divided by the average price in inventory.


### **Inventory valuation**


Inventory valuation is the accounting process of assigning a monetary value to unsold stock at the end of an accounting period. Inventory valuation helps retailers maximize profitability and keep financial statements accurate. Retailers calculate this figure using established methods like FIFO (First-In, First-Out), LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) or weighted average cost.


### **Just-in-time (JIT) inventory**


[Just-in-time inventory (JIT)](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/just-in-time-inventory-management/) is a strategy where retailers receive inventory just as it’s needed to sell to customers, rather than storing large amounts of stock ahead of time. It is one of several techniques retailers use for managing inventory. JIT helps retailers reduce dead stock risk and storage costs, but it requires accurate forecasting to avoid stockouts.


### **Last-mile delivery**


Last-mile delivery refers to the final step of the delivery process, where an order travels from a distribution point directly to the customer’s doorstep or pickup location. It is typically the most expensive portion of shipping. For retailers, it can include deliveries from a store, courier handoffs or local delivery partners.


### **LIFO (Last In, First Out)**


[LIFO](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-is-lifo/) (Last In, First Out) is an inventory management method where the newest inventory is sold first. Unlike FIFO, LIFO is usually used by businesses selling non-perishable goods. In periods of inflation, using the cost of newer, higher-priced inventory increases your cost of goods sold (COGS), helping you reduce taxable income and improve cash flow.


### **Order lead time**


The order lead time is the period between when the retailer places an order with a supplier and when the product is delivered to their store.


### **Overstocking**


[Overstocking](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/manage-surplus-overstock-inventory/) means holding more inventory than a retailer can reasonably sell within the expected period. When you overbuy and undersell inventory, it ties up your cash flow and storage space. A retailer can identify overstock by comparing on-hand quantities with recent sales and forecast demand.


There are many ways to manage overstock inventory. You can simply discount it, transfer it to higher-demand locations or offload it through an inventory liquidator.


### **Quantity on hand or on order**


If merchandise is on hand, it means that the retailer has it in their possession. If something is on order, this is stock that retailers have on open purchase orders or manufacturing orders.


### **Reorder point**


[Reorder point](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/reorder-point-formula/) is the inventory level at which a new purchase order should be placed, so you don’t run out of inventory while waiting for replenishment. For example, if a product sells steadily while a delivery takes several weeks, the reorder point should cover that demand before new stock arrives.


Modern POS systems like Lightspeed include automated reordering capabilities. When your inventory reaches its reorder point, the system will place a new purchase order to the vendor automatically so you don’t have to do it manually.


### **Reverse logistics**


Reverse logistics is the movement of products from the end customer back through the supply chain to the retailer or manufacturer. Examples include customer returns, repairs, exchanges, recycling and product recalls. Having a well-designed reverse logistics process is important for retailers as it allows them to quickly inspect, repackage and restock returned items to the sales floor.


### **Safety stock**


[Safety stock](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-is-safety-stock/) is extra stock retailers arrange to make sure they don’t run out of inventory. It is usually held as a buffer to protect against situations like unexpected demand increase or delayed supplier shipment. Having safety stock helps ensure that customers aren’t disappointed and you can continue to meet their expectations. Setting the safety stock level too low can increase stockout risk, while setting it too high adds carrying costs.


### **Stock keeping unit (SKU)**


A[stock-keeping unit](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/sku-numbers/) (SKU) is an identification code that’s often displayed as a machine-readable barcode that allows retailers to keep track of items in their inventory. An SKU doesn’t need to be assigned to physical products that are in the retailer’s inventory and can be assigned to intangible products such as repairs or warranties.


### **Stockout**


[Stockouts](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-are-stockouts/) happen when a product a customer wants is unavailable for purchase, either in a store or online. It can result from unexpectedly high demand, late supplier deliveries, inaccurate inventory records or a missed reorder. For retailers, stockouts mean lost sales and disappointed customers who may shop elsewhere.


Retailers can prevent stockouts by using a[POS inventory management system](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/inventory-management-software/) . For example, Lightspeed POS lets you track stock in real time and set reorder points or min/max levels across core products, so you always know what to restock and when.


### **Supply chain management**


[Supply chain management](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/retail-supply-chain-management/) is the range of activities necessary to plan, control, and deliver a product. It encompasses the acquisition of raw materials and producing the item to the distribution of the goods to the final customer. All this must be done in the most efficient way possible.


### **Wholesale**


Selling[wholesale](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/B2B-wholesale-platform/) means that you generally sell your product in bulk quantities to a “middleman” who then goes on to sell it to the consumer or in some instances other retailers. Due to high-volume purchase orders, wholesalers are typically able to buy products from manufacturers at a lower price and add their margins.


## **Retail pricing and merchandising terms**


### **Assortment planning**


[Assortment planning](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/assortment-planning/) is a process of deciding which products a retailer will offer in a store. When planning assortment, retailers consider not only the product type. They also look at color, size, price, SKU and other characteristics, while also taking into account historical sales and local customer demographics. Smart assortment planning is essential for optimizing sales.


### **Bundled pricing**


Bundled pricing is the sale of goods and services at a lower price than they would be charged if they were all purchased separately. Popular examples of[bundled pricing](https://smallbusiness.chron.com/bundle-pricing-strategy-67049.html) include option packages on new cars, meal deals at restaurants and cable TV channel plans. Implementing a bundled pricing strategy can allow you to increase your profit by giving customers a discount on items that aren’t selling well individually.


### **Category management**


Category management is the practice of grouping similar products together into distinct categories and managing each group as a business unit. Instead of looking at every single item in a store one by one, a retailer looks at a whole group–like “breakfast cereal,” “shampoo” or “pet food”–to decide which products to sell, how to price them, how much shelf space to give them and when to put them on sale.


### **Cross merchandising**


When retailers display unrelated products from different categories together, this is known as cross merchandising. Products are grouped in imaginative ways, often connected by a common theme or event, to encourage customers to see a relationship between them and purchase all of them.


Examples of cross merchandising can be as simple as selling batteries next to electronic goods or light bulbs next to lamps. They can also be more elaborate, like selling grills together with all the food, utensils and dishes needed for grilled cheese sandwiches.


### **Depth of assortment**


This is the amount of each item or different styles of a product that a retailer stocks. For example, a store may want to keep inventory costs down and as such have a shallow product depth, meaning that they may only have 3-5 different types of each product in stock.


### **Dynamic pricing**


[Dynamic pricing](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/the-art-of-dynamic-pricing/) is a pricing strategy where retailers change the price of a product or service in response to certain conditions, such as demand, time, inventory levels or competition. For example, a winter jacket costs more in winter than at the end of spring, while sunscreen costs more during a July heatwave than in November. Retailers use dynamic pricing to increase revenue and profit margins. On the other hand, it might cause customer frustration.


### **Endcap display**


An endcap display is a product display placed at the end of a store aisle, where it is visible to shoppers from the main walkway. Retailers often use endcaps to place seasonal goods, promotions, new arrivals or complementary products. Because the location attracts heavy foot traffic, endcap displays encourage product discovery and add-on purchases.


### **Flash sales**


A[flash sale](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-is-flash-sale/) is a promotion or discount offered by a store, either ecommerce or brick-and-mortar, for a brief period. Because the quantity of the goods is limited, higher discounts are offered in comparison to frequent promotions. This encourages impulse buying as the time limit and limited availability entices customers to make a purchase through fear of missing out on a bargain.


### **Hardlines and softlines**


Also known as hard goods and soft goods,[hardlines and softlines](https://smallbusiness.chron.com/retail-hardlines-softlines-76200.html) are two major kinds of retail inventory. Soft goods are items that are literally soft, such as clothing. Hard goods are non-personal items such as electronics, appliances and sporting equipment.


### **Loss leader**


[Loss leaders](https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/knowledge/strategy/loss-leader-pricing/) are goods or services that are offered at significantly discounted rates, sometimes even below cost, to attract customers into a store and to promote sales. It is a tried and trusted method of enticing customers into stores and has been met with much success, especially by larger discount retailers. The idea behind this pricing strategy is that the customer will buy the loss leader item and other products from within the store that are not discounted.


### **MAP pricing**


MAP pricing stands for Minimum Advertised Price. It is the lowest price set by a manufacturer or brand at which a retailer may publicly display or advertise a product. While retailers can technically negotiate a lower final sale price in-person, they cannot display below-MAP pricing in ads, storefront windows or ecommerce listings. MAP policies protect a brand’s value, keep profits healthy and stop big retailers from underselling smaller local shops.


### **Markdown and markup**


Markdowns are the discounts that retailers make on merchandise from the original marked price. Unlike sales or promotional events, a markdown is when the list price is changed to a lower price permanently. Goods that aren’t selling very well are usually marked down. Markup is the amount by which the cost of a product is increased to derive the selling price.


### **Merchandising**


Merchandising is any practice that helps to facilitate the sale of goods to a customer. This term refers to a range of marketing strategies where retailers present goods and services to potential customers in the most appealing and convincing way possible, to entice them to part with their hard-earned money. How products are merchandised determines how likely a retailer can sell them. By following best practices, it’s more likely that customers will want to spend money.


### **Planogram**


A[planogram](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/planogram-in-retail/) is a diagram that demonstrates how and where products should be displayed in a retail store to increase the number of purchases that a customer makes. Planograms are a vital part of merchandising and retail space planning. Planograms are sometimes used by manufacturers to suggest the most effective displays for their merchandise at stores.


### **Planogram compliance**


Planogram compliance describes how closely a retail store’s physical shelf layout matches the approved visual diagram (the planogram) provided for its shelves and displays. Planograms dictate the exact shelf placement, number of facings and vertical orientation for every SKU. Following a planogram helps retailers ensure consistent presentation across locations and make products easier to find for shoppers.


### **Prestige pricing**


A[marketing strategy](https://blog.hubspot.com/sales/prestige-pricing) where prices are set higher than usual because lower prices would hurt the brand identity instead of helping with sales. For example, with high-end perfume and clothing. There are a certain set of consumers who believe that if the price is set high then it denotes the quality and prestige of said item. Luxury products meet the expectations of this niche group of customers who seek to satisfy their desire for a higher social status by owning the product.


### **Private label**


A product is considered part of a[private label](https://www.business.com/articles/private-labeling-details/) when it is manufactured by a third party but sold under the brand name of the retailer. A benefit to this is that the retailer gets to specify everything about the product from the ingredients and packaging to the label. This contrasts with buying products manufactured by other companies that come adorned with their brand names.


### **Product life cycle**


This describes the stages that a product goes through from when it was simply an idea until it’s removed from the market. Not all products reach the final stage, some will continue to grow from strength to strength while others rise and fall. Businesses try to extend the life cycle of their products by launching advertising campaigns or reducing the price.


### **Psychological pricing**


Psychological pricing is a[pricing strategy](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/the-art-of-pricing-strategies-to-maximise-profits-without-alienating-customers/) retailers use to influence customers to spend more money through different techniques, like getting the best price point or getting the best quality. The key is to make the customer feel as though they made a successful purchase. Common examples are setting a price at $9.99 rather than $10, which may be perceived as lower, or using a premium price, which signals exclusivity.


### **Quantity discount**


This is an incentive that’s offered to the buyer whereby purchasing an item in bulk will result in a reduced price per unit. Sometimes it’s only a minuscule difference, but a difference nonetheless. Seeking out quantity discounts can make a world of difference to small and up-and-coming businesses.


### **Retail markup percentage**


[Retail markup](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/markup-vs-margin/) percentage shows how much a product’s selling price exceeds its cost, expressed as a percentage of cost. To find the markup percentage, retailers use this equation: ((Selling price – Cost) / Cost) x 100. For example, if you buy a shirt for $20 and sell it for $40, you added a 100% markup. Retailers use markup when setting product prices, but it’s not the same as profit margin, which represents revenue they retain as profit.


### **Seasonal merchandising**


Seasonal merchandising is used to present and sell products around seasons, holidays, cultural events or weather shifts. For example, a retailer may feature giftable products before Christmas or Valentine’s Day. Retailers usually plan seasonal merchandising months ahead. It includes choosing inventory, timing promotions and arranging displays so products are visible and available when shoppers want them.


### **Visual hierarchy**


Visual hierarchy is a strategic placement of visual elements to direct shoppers’ attention purposefully, so they notice the most important information or products first. In a store, retailers can use size, color, contrast, placement and lighting to draw attention to a featured product, price or promotion. Visual hierarchy is also used to make displays easier to scan.


### **Visual merchandising**


[Visual merchandising](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/visual-merchandising/) is the act of creating appealing displays that will cause the customer to purchase goods. This is proven to be an effective means of driving foot traffic and sales. Effective visual merchandising will bring customers into the store and encourage them to make purchases. Visual merchandising begins on the outside of the store, often with attractive window displays, to entice the customer to come inside.


## **Checkout and payment terms**


### **Buy now, pay later (BNPL)**


[Buy now, pay later (BNPL)](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/retailers-buy-now-pay-later/) is a payment option that lets customers receive a purchase immediately and pay for it later, often through installments. A retailer may offer BNPL at online or in-store checkout to give shoppers another way to pay. Offering BNPL helps retailers increase conversion rates and average order value. On the downside, however, BNPL providers charge merchants fees, which are typically higher than traditional credit card fees.


### **Card-not-present transaction (CNP)**


[Card-not-present transaction (CNP)](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/card-not-present-transaction/) is any transaction using a credit card when the physical card is not presented to the retailer. That includes online mobile and desktop sales, mail order and phone transactions, as well as transactions where a card number is keyed in. Because the physical card can’t be checked in person, CNP transactions may carry more fraud risks than card-present transactions.


### **Chargeback**


A[chargeback](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/credit-card-chargebacks/) is a charge that’s returned to a payment card after a customer successfully disputes a purchase on their account. A chargeback can occur on bank accounts or credit cards. They are issued to the cardholder for a variety of reasons such as when a customer decides to return an item, if a merchant duplicates a charge in error, or if a technical issue occurs that causes a card to be charged incorrectly. A chargeback is a refund as it returns funds taken from an account to pay for a prior purchase.


### **Cloud POS**


A[cloud POS](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/cloud-pos-system/) is a modern point-of-sale system that runs over the internet and stores transaction data, product catalogs and customer records on remote cloud servers rather than on-premises hardware. With a cloud POS system, retail store owners can log into their back office from any web browser, manage products centrally and receive automatic software updates. Plus, compared to traditional POS, cloud POS systems are cheaper to implement and easier to scale.


### **Contactless payments**


[Contactless payments](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/contactless-payments/) let a customer pay by tapping a compatible card, phone or smartwatch near a payment terminal, without having to insert or swipe a card. Tap-to-pay credit or debit cards and mobile wallets like Apple Pay and Google Pay are some of the most common examples of contactless payment methods. For retailers, offering contactless payment options helps increase checkout speed and shorten queue lines.


### **Digital wallet**


A digital wallet is an application on a smartphone or a smartwatch that stores a user’s payment information (credit card, debit card or bank account number). It allows users to pay for purchases directly from their devices instead of using a physical card or having to manually enter their card and billing information at checkout.


Apple Pay, Google Pay and Amazon Pay are some of the most popular digital wallets. Retailers accept digital wallets to reduce checkout friction and minimize input errors.


### **EMV chip card**


EMV chip card contains a computer chip that helps authenticate a payment transaction. EMV refers to the standards developed by Europay, Mastercard and Visa and adopted broadly across payment systems. For retail stores, accepting chip cards can reduce in-person card fraud, protect the business from the cost of fake cards and give shoppers a safer way to pay.


### **Integrated payments**


[Integrated payments](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/payment-processing-integrated-vs-non-integrated/) connect a store’s point-of-sale (POS) system directly to its card reader, automatically syncing sales data and payment approvals. This means staff don’t have to manually re-enter information into a standalone terminal, which prevents mistakes, speeds up checkout and makes it much easier to balance the books at the end of the day.


### **Layaway**


Layaway, also known as lay-by, works differently than shopping with traditional means like credit cards or installment billing plans. When on a layaway plan you make the payments over a prearranged period, but unlike when you pay by credit card, your goods will stay in the store until you’ve finished paying for them in full.


### **Mobile payments**


Mobile payments are sent or received from a mobile device. Mobile payments are an alternative to paying with cash, credit cards, or check. Some merchants prefer to enable mobile payments in their business since it simplifies the payment process for customers, making the checkout process a more seamless experience.


### **Mobile POS (mPOS)**


A mobile POS (mPOS) is a portable point-of-sale solution that runs on a smartphone or tablet paired with a mobile card reader and POS software. Lightspeed’s[mobile POS system](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/mobile-pos-system/) is one example.


With a mobile POS system, retail staff can look up inventory, process sales, accept credit card payments and email receipts anywhere on the sales floor without having to rely on a fixed cash register counter. Retailers use mobile POS to reduce checkout lines during busy periods or when running[pop-up shops](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/pop-up-shop/) .


### **Payment gateway**


[Payment gateway](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/understanding-payment-gateways/) is the technology that securely passes a customer’s payment information to the payment processor for authorization and ensuring it gets where it needs to go safely and quickly. It acts as a bridge between the customer, the retailer and their banks. Modern payment gateways typically support credit cards, debit cards and digital wallets.


### **PCI compliance**


The set of guidelines known as the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) applies to companies that accept payments by credit card, regardless of the size of the business. Any company that accepts card payments and stores, processes and transmits cardholder data, must host that data securely with a hosting provider that is PCI compliant.


### **Point of sale (POS) system**


In its simplest form, a[point of sale system](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/) is a cash register that allows retailers to ring up sales and keep track of their transactions. More modern setups feature a computer and monitor, a cash drawer, a receipt printer, customer display and a barcode scanner. Most POS systems also feature a credit and debit card reader.


### **Price look up**


Known as a PLU, price look up codes are 4 or 5-digit numbers which have been used by supermarkets since 1990 to make checkout and inventory control easier, more efficient and more accurate. It’s an effective system that displays the description and price of an item when the item number is entered or scanned at the point of sale. They ensure that the correct price is paid by consumers by removing the need for cashiers to attempt to identify the product.


### **Tokenization**


Tokenization is a payment security protocol that replaces sensitive customer credit card details with a unique, randomly generated digital identifier known as a “token”. A retailer may use tokens to support saved cards or recurring payments without storing the full card number. Tokenization helps keep payment data safe. Even if a store’s system gets hacked, hackers can’t work backward to steal real card or bank numbers.


## **Ecommerce and omnichannel retail terms**


### **Cart abandonment**


Cart abandonment happens when online shoppers add one or more items to their shopping cart but leave before finalizing their purchase. While **the global average cart abandonment rate is nearly 70%** , there are many tactics merchants can implement to prevent cart abandonment. These include being upfront about the total cost, offering free shipping, simplifying the checkout process, offering a guest checkout option, providing flexible payment options, adding social proof and more.


### **Click and collect**


Known by many other names like scheduled pickup, curbside pickup and product pickup, click and collect refers to the act of ordering something online and then collecting from the physical store. Customers are increasingly choosing this over delivery service because it offers the immediate gratification of receiving their item, while also saving money on delivery.


The COVID-19 pandemic made this feature absolutely essential, and normalized the experience for reluctant shoppers. Retailers can benefit from click and collect also, as it reduces the cost of operation and can influence customers into making impulse purchases when they visit your store. The in-store collection also offers an opportunity for retailers to connect with customers on a personal level, improving the overall customer experience.


### **Direct-to-consumer (DTC)**


[Direct-to-consumer (DTC)](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/dtc-marketing/) is a retail sales model where a brand sells its products directly to end consumers without wholesalers, distributors or third-party retailers. They can sell through their own ecommerce website, app, social media or brand-owned physical stores. A DTC brand has complete control over branding, customer service and customer data. Examples of DTC brands include Warby Parker, Allbirds and Glossier.


### **Endless aisle**


An[endless aisle](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/endless-aisle-in-retail-how-it-works-and-best-practices/) refers to a brick-and-mortar store that allows customers to peruse the entire catalog with minimal effort. Instead of stocking up on every item and expecting the client to spend their precious time browsing endless shelves, the retailer provides the entire catalogue to browse on a touchscreen or a tablet.


### **E-tailing**


Short for electronic retailing and usually referred to by its more common name,[ecommerce](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/ecom/) , e-tailing refers to the sale of goods and services through the internet. It can include business-to-business sales of products and services as well as business-to-customer. This is achieved through advertising and subscriptions to website content. This method of sales requires detailed product and service displays and descriptions to give shoppers an accurate idea of the look and quality of the products without them needing to be in a physical store.


### **Marketplace selling**


Marketplace selling is the practice of listing and selling products on third-party platforms like Amazon, eBay or Etsy that bring together multiple sellers. This gives retailers instant access to a wider audience without having to bring in their own traffic. But they usually must follow platform rules, pay commission fees on every sale and battle the competition.


### **Mobile shopping**


This is the act of shopping on a mobile device, like a smartphone or tablet. This has become increasingly popular in recent years due to many websites being optimized for display on mobile devices and tablets. It’s virtually the same as shopping on a desktop PC or a laptop, only with a smaller screen.


### **Multichannel retail**


Multichannel retail means selling through more than one channel, such as a physical store, an ecommerce site, marketplaces or social platforms. While each channel gives customers another way to discover and buy products, these channels may operate on separate systems, creating data silos for teams and disconnected experiences for shoppers.


### **Omnichannel retail**


[Omnichannel retailing](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/omnichannel-retail/) , also known as omnichannel commerce, is an approach to sales that aims to give customers a fluid shopping experience whatever the means they are using to shop. Whether they’re buying from an ecommerce store, over the phone or in a traditional brick-and-mortar store. This approach utilizes multiple means of promoting and distributing goods. For example, websites and apps, phone calls, emails and social media.


### **Showrooming**


Showrooming is when a customer will visit a store to see a product in the flesh but then goes on to purchase it from an online retailer. This happens because many people prefer seeing first-hand what they are going to buy, but things are often available cheaper from online vendors. Because of this, their local retailer essentially becomes a showroom for them.


### **Social commerce**


[Social commerce](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/social-commerce/) is defined as the ability to make a purchase from a third-party company within the social media experience. An example of this would be browsing and comparing products on a business’ Facebook page and then making the purchase directly through Facebook, as opposed to being redirected to the company’s website to complete the transaction. Similarly, a potential customer may see a Tweet about a product and then be able to purchase it directly via Twitter instead of being redirected to the retailer’s own website.


### **Subscription commerce**


Subscription commerce is a business model where customers receive products or services on a recurring schedule through automatic payments. For example, a retailer might offer regular deliveries of coffee, pet food or skincare items. This model helps retailers generate predictable recurring revenue and increase customer lifetime value by turning single transactions into repeating purchases.


### **Webrooming**


The opposite of showrooming, webrooming refers to the act of looking at a product online before venturing out to a physical store and purchasing it from there. Customers sometimes choose to do this as it allows them to see goods in the flesh before deciding to make the purchase.


## **Retail marketing and analytics terms**


### **Average order value (AOV)**


[Average order value](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/how-to-increase-average-order-value/) (AOV) is the average amount customers spend each time they complete a purchase. You can calculate it by dividing total sales revenue by the number of orders in the same period. To increase AOV, retailers and ecommerce merchants often use strategies like product bundles, free shipping thresholds or cross-selling.


### **ATS**


ATS stands for average transaction size, which is the average amount spent on a single transaction or purchase. It’s calculated by dividing the value of sales during a given time by the number of transactions in that same period. This data is invaluable in measuring sales growth over time.


### **Basket size**


Basket size refers to the number of products a customer purchases in a single transaction. You can calculate it by dividing the total number of units sold by the total number of order transactions. Unlike average order value, which measures monetary spend, basket size evaluates merchandise volume. This metric is used to measure the effectiveness of visual merchandising, upselling and product bundling.


### **Big data**


For most retail businesses, profit margins are small and keeping a close eye on overhead and delivery costs is a vital part of maintaining profitability. Finding ways to attract new customers and build brand loyalty is a constant challenge.


Big data can help a business to understand a customer’s desires. By collecting and combining data from sales, inventory, revenue and other sources, big data analysts can help a retailer hone their operations and reduce operating costs, boost customer satisfaction and increase the likelihood that they will return, and generate more profits.


### **Clienteling**


Clienteling is the set of processes that retailers can utilize to increase customer value by delivering them a personalized, more intimate shopping experience. The sophisticated technology and software necessary for accurate clienteling is gradually becoming more affordable, making the practice more widespread.


Modern clienteling solutions can deliver in-depth data to a business, allowing them to provide a personalized experience to each customer and generate a rapid return on their investment in technology and training.


### **Conversion funnel**


A conversion funnel describes the steps a potential customer takes from first discovering a retailer or product to completing a purchase. Retailers often measure how many shoppers progress or leave at each stage to find where friction happens. Common stages include **awareness** (top of funnel), **interest and consideration** (middle of funnel), **conversion** (bottom of funnel) and **retention** (post-conversion).


### **Conversion rates**


[Retail conversion rates](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/how-to-improve-conversion-rates-in-your-retail-store/) measure the percentage of visitors that make a purchase. For example, if 100 shoppers visit a store but only 20 make a purchase, the conversion rate is 20 percent. To accurately measure retail conversion, you must count the people who enter a store but also take into consideration partners, children, and visitors, such as sales representatives or maintenance staff, who do not represent potential shoppers.


### **Customer acquisition cost (CAC)**


[Customer acquisition cost](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/customer-acquisition-cost/) (CAC) is the average amount a business spends to gain a new customer over a specific period. To calculate CAC, divide your total sales and marketing costs by the number of new customers acquired in that period. For example, if you spent $2000 on marketing last month and gained 200 new customers, your CAC is $10 per customer.


Retailers usually measure CAC against Customer Lifetime Value (CLV). The ratio should be around three to one, which means you should earn $3 in lifetime revenue for every dollar you spend to acquire a customer.


### **Customer journey**


Customer journey is the sequence of interactions a person has with a retailer before, during and after a purchase across different channels. It may include seeing an ad, browsing a retailer’s website, completing a purchase through the retailer’s app, interacting with a customer support representative and returning an item in-store. Mapping the customer journey helps retailers find gaps and optimize operations to deliver a more consistent customer experience.


### **Customer lifetime value (CLV)**


[Customer lifetime value](https://retail-support.lightspeedhq.com/hc/en-us/articles/7294497443611-Understanding-Customer-Lifetime-Value) (CLV) estimates the revenue or profit a business can expect to earn from a customer over the entire relationship. It looks at how valuable a customer is to the business as a whole, not just during a single transaction.


Retailers can measure CLV in two ways. The first one is a **historical CLV** that looks at how much an existing customer has already spent with the business, while the second one is a **predictive CLV** that is an estimate of how much a customer might spend.


### **Customer retention**


Customer retention is a retailer’s ability to keep existing customers and continue to generate revenue from them. Modern retailers focus on customer retention because[statistically](https://hbr.org/2014/10/the-value-of-keeping-the-right-customers) , **acquiring a new customer can cost up to 25 times more than keeping an existing one** . They usually increase customer retention by offering loyalty programs and providing personalized customer experiences.


### **Demand generation**


Demand generation is the set of marketing activities designed to create awareness and interest in a retailer’s products among potential customers. Those may include blog content, email campaigns, events, partnerships, social media ads and more. Instead of focusing on driving immediate purchases, demand generation activities introduce a brand, educate shoppers and warm up potential customers to support later conversion.


### **Geofencing**


Geofencing is a location-based digital marketing technology that sets a virtual geographic perimeter around a specific physical location. When mobile users with location services enabled cross this invisible boundary, a retailer sends them push notifications, promotional discounts or mobile ads to attract local foot traffic directly into the storefront.


### **Gross margin**


A business’ gross margin is its total sales revenue minus the[cost of goods sold](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-is-cogs/) , divided by its total sales revenue and then expressed as a percentage. The percent of total sales revenue that the company keeps after dealing with the direct costs of producing and selling the products that it sells is the gross margin. The higher the percentage, the more that the company makes from each sale.


### **Gross merchandise value (GMV)**


Gross merchandise value (GMV) is the total value of all goods or services sold through a platform or marketplace over a specific period, before deducting expenses, customer returns or processing fees. You can calculate GMV by multiplying the sale price of each item by the total number of items sold. Tracking GMV is important because it shows whether your overall sales volume and customer demand are growing.


### **Heat mapping**


Heat mapping is a data visualization technique that shows where activity is concentrated, such as customer movement through a store or clicks on a webpage. In a physical store, a retailer might use aggregated sensor or camera data to see which areas attract attention and which are overlooked by shoppers. Retailers use heatmaps alongside other tools to optimize store layouts.


### **Impulse purchases**


An impulse purchase is a thing that a customer purchases with no prior plan, often because of a sudden whim or impulse. A customer who makes this kind of purchase is considered an impulse purchaser or buyer.


### **Loyalty program**


A loyalty program rewards customers for repeat purchases through discounts, member pricing, personalized offers, exclusive gifts, special benefits and other perks. The aim is to encourage repeat visits, increase average order value and improve customer retention. Some common types of loyalty programs for retail stores include points-based programs, tiered programs, paid (membership) programs, cashback programs and referral programs.


### **Monthly sales index**


This is a measure of seasonal sales that can be calculated by dividing each month’s sales by the average monthly sales and then multiplying that number by 100. Any result higher than 100 means that there has been growth. If it’s less than 100, then that month there has been a loss.


### **Relationship retailing**


When a business seeks to establish and maintain long-term bonds with customers, rather than treat each sales transaction as a completely new encounter with them, this is known as relationship retailing. This often manifests itself in the form of loyalty programs and fantastic customer service.


### **Retail analytics**


Retail analytics is the process of collecting and analyzing sales, inventory, customer, operations and other data to understand performance and guide decisions. For example, tools like[Lightspeed Insights](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/analytics/) , which is part of Lightspeed’s retail analytics module, can provide retailers with detailed data about inventory performance, employee performance and customer behavior. With this data on hand, retailers can make better business decisions.


### **Retail KPIs**


[Retail KPIs](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/retail-kpi/) (key performance indicators) are quantitative metrics retailers use to evaluate how their business is performing and optimize operational efficiency. Common retail KPIs include conversion rate, sales per square foot, average transaction value, inventory turnover, gross margin and customer retention. Retailers typically track these metrics through their[POS analytics and reporting](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/report-with-retail-pos-system/) tools.


### **Retargeting**


Retargeting is a digital advertising strategy that shows ads to people who have previously interacted with a retailer. For example, they have visited a retailer’s website or mobile app and added an item to a shopping cart but haven’t finished a purchase. Retargeting ads can be displayed on different marketing channels like paid search, social platforms and display networks. These ads show shoppers the exact items they left in their carts, reminding them to return and complete their purchase.


### **Return on investment (ROI)**


Return on investment (ROI) compares the financial return from an activity with its cost. Retailers calculate ROI by dividing net profit by the initial cost to see if projects (like remodeling a store or running social media ads) are worth the money. A strong, positive ROI proves that their spending is actually growing the business.


### **Sell-through rate**


[Sell-through rate](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/sell-through-rate/) is a retail metric that measures the percentage of inventory sold during a specific time period compared to the total stock a retailer purchased from a manufacturer or supplier. You can calculate it by dividing the number of units sold by the number of units received, then multiplying it by 100. In general, retailers track sell-through rate to understand how quickly inventory is moving.


### **Store loyalty**


When a customer likes and trusts a store, and continually makes purchases there without being swayed by advertising or special offers, this is known as store loyalty. Retailers can encourage this by offering rewards programs or special discounts for regular customers. A good example of this would be the Starbucks loyalty card, where customers are offered free drinks.


### **Units per transaction**


Shortened to UPT, units per transaction is the metric that measures how many items a customer purchases in any given transaction. It can be calculated daily or over a longer period. This is an important metric that helps measure the growth of a business, as well as employee effectiveness in certain retail environments.


## **Sustainability and ethical retail terms**


### **Carbon-neutral shipping**


Carbon-neutral shipping is a way of delivering products to customers where the emissions created during shipping are balanced out, resulting in a net-zero carbon footprint. Retailers usually do this by funding verified carbon offset projects (like tree planting or renewable energy) or simply by using electric delivery vehicles.


### **Circular retail**


Circular retail is a retail model where products and materials are reused, repurposed and recycled. For example, a retailer might offer repair services, refurbishment, resale, refill options or material recycling. These practices help retailers reduce waste, extend the lifecycle of their products and appeal to eco-conscious shoppers.


### **Ethical sourcing**


Ethical sourcing means selecting suppliers and products with attention to how goods are made and how workers, communities, animals and the environment are treated. But primarily, ethical sourcing focuses on human rights, labor conditions and fair treatment of employees. Retailers often highlight ethical sourcing certifications to earn customer trust.


### **Green retailing**


Green retailing is an increasingly popular approach towards managing a retail business by implementing environmentally friendly and sustainable practices and processes. By implementing such processes, retail businesses can become more efficient and save money in the process.


### **Green supply chain**


Green supply chain uses eco-friendly practices at every stage of production and delivery, from sourcing materials and manufacturing to shipping orders to customers. Retailers do this by using solar energy in distribution centers, optimizing delivery routes to save fuel and partnering with eco-friendly carriers. The goal is to reduce environmental impact.


### **Recommerce**


Recommerce (also known as *reverse commerce* ) refers to the reselling of previously owned, returned, refurbished or open-box items through online and physical stores. Many apparel, outdoor gear and electronics brands now manage their own recommerce platforms, where customers can trade in used items for store credit. Recommerce gives customers quality items at lower prices, while retailers earn extra revenue and reduce waste.


### **Sustainable packaging**


Sustainable packaging (also referred to as *green packaging* or *eco-friendly packaging* ) is packaging designed to have minimal impact on the environment. This usually involves using right-sized boxes, biodegradable materials, reusable containers or materials that can be recycled. Some examples of sustainable packaging materials include biodegradable plastic, recycled paper and glass.


## **Retail technology terms**


### **Augmented reality**


Often shortened to AR, this principle is about supplementing the customer’s physical world with virtual things, so they appear to be in the same environment. In retail, AR can be used in shoppable catalogues, apps that let you see in-store deals by using your phone’s camera and virtual fitting rooms. While this is still relatively new technology, it is set to become more widespread in coming years.


### **Computer vision**


Computer vision is a field of AI that enables software to interpret information from images or video. In retail stores, it may be used to analyze shelf availability, count people, support self-checkout, enable virtual try-ons or identify safety issues. The performance of computer vision systems, however, greatly depends on image quality and the setting in which it is used.


### **ERP system**


An ERP system is an enterprise resource planning system that brings together a retailer’s core business operations into a single centralized database. Key functions and modules typically include supply chain and procurement, finance and accounting, workforce management, sales and customer management. An ERP system helps retailers eliminate data silos and provides real-time visibility into all operations, processes and performance.


### **Internet of Things (IoT) in retail**


The Internet of Things (IoT) in retail refers to a physical network of connected devices that share data over the internet. These include, for example, RFID scanners, digital shelf tags, climate sensors and cameras. In retail stores, IoT technology is used to track stock in real time, monitor temperature-sensitive grocery items, support frictionless checkout and personalize in-store experiences.


### **Radio-frequency identification**


Usually shortened to RFID, radio-frequency identification is the use of radio waves to read and capture information stored on a tag. A tag can be read from several feet away and doesn’t need to be directly in front of the reader to be tracked. Retailers can use RFID tags to help record information, including stock quantity and precise locations of items.


### **Retail automation**


Retail automation means using technology to handle repetitive tasks with minimal human effort. It can be applied across areas like inventory management (e.g., automated reorders), checkout and payments (e.g., self-checkout kiosks), pricing and merchandising (e.g., automated price updates), marketing (e.g., product recommendations) and customer service (e.g., customer support chatbots). Retail automation helps retailers reduce human error and speed up repetitive work.


### **Retail CRM**


A retail CRM is a customer relationship management system retailers use to organize and store customer information, such as purchase histories, contact details, communication logs and marketing preferences. Store associates and marketing teams use CRM data to personalize customer interactions, segment marketing campaigns and send loyalty promotions.


### **Smart shelves**


Smart shelves are retail shelves fitted with technologies like weight sensors and RFID (radio-frequency identification) tags that can detect product presence, quantity or movement. These technologies help retailers monitor inventory levels on shelves in real time, timely identify low stock and alert store staff the moment an item is misplaced or runs out of stock.


### **Warehouse management system**


A[warehouse management system (WMS)](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/features-of-retail-warehouse-management-software/) refers to software and general processes that let organizations manage and administer warehouse operations from the time goods or materials enter a warehouse until they move out.


## **Commonly confused retail terms**


### **Integrated payments vs payment gateways**


Integrated payments connect a retailer’s payment processing directly to its point-of-sale (POS) system so transaction details sync with sales records automatically. A payment gateway securely moves payment information from a checkout interface to the processor for authorization. A payment gateway can be one part of an integrated payments setup, but the terms are not interchangeable.


### **Markup vs markdown**


Markup and markdown move product price in different directions. Markup is the percentage added to a product’s wholesale cost to establish its retail price and generate profit. Markdown is a reduction from a product’s original selling price. Retailers usually use markdowns to move slow-selling items or clear seasonal stock.


### **Omnichannel retail vs multichannel retail**


Both omnichannel and multichannel retail models enable retailers to sell their products across more than one channel (stores, ecommerce, marketplaces), but they have operational differences. In multichannel retail, channels usually operate and are managed separately. For shoppers, it can create a disconnected experience. In omnichannel retail, retailers aim to connect every sales channel to provide shoppers with a more seamless, unified experience no matter where and how they shop.


### **Showrooming vs webrooming**


Showrooming is when a shopper examines a product in a physical store and then buys it online. Showroomers often look for lower prices and online discounts. Webrooming is when a shopper researches a product online and then visits a store to purchase it. Webroomers usually want to test fit or product quality before buying and avoid shipping fees.


## **Emerging retail terms and trends to watch**


### **AI in retail**


[AI in retail](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/ai-in-retail/) refers to the usage of Artificial Intelligence in retail operations to automate or optimize manual processes. Common AI in retail use cases include inventory management, merchandising, product recommendations, dynamic pricing, reporting, demand forecasting, content or image generation and AI chatbots for customer support.


For example,[Lightspeed AI](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/ai/) can provide retailers with instant insights about performance and recommend next-best actions. It can also complete tasks for you (such as creating purchase orders or stock transfers), with your approval.


#### A retailer’s playbook for adopting AI


Discover how to leverage AI without losing the human touch. Backed by Lightspeed's research, this guide explores where AI delivers real value, where it falls short and how to strike the right balance.


[Download the AI in Retail Guide](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/resources/retail/ai-retail-guide/)


### **Headless commerce**


Headless commerce is an ecommerce architecture where the customer-facing front-end (the **“head”,** such as a website or mobile app) is completely separated from the back-end commerce engine (the **“body”** ) that manages products, carts, orders and payments. The two sides communicate through APIs. This allows a retailer to build or change front-end experiences without replacing the underlying commerce engine.


### **Retail media networks (RMN)**


A retail media network (RMN) is an advertising platform owned by a retailer that allows third-party brands to purchase targeted digital ads across the retailer’s website, mobile app, email newsletters and in-store digital screens. With RMN, advertisers get access to relevant audiences, while retailers can create a new revenue stream for their business.


### **Smart stores**


Smart stores are physical stores that use various technologies to create a more engaging environment for consumers, improve the shopping experience, optimize operations and grow revenue. Examples include digital shelf labels, sensors, cashierless checkout, intelligent inventory tools, lighting systems and more. Smart store technologies also enable retailers to deliver more personalized experiences to shoppers.


### **Unified commerce**


Unified commerce is a retail architecture that connects a retailer’s backend systems (including inventory, point of sale, orders, customer data and ecommerce) into a single centralized platform. Unlike multichannel and omnichannel setups where systems can operate in silos, unified commerce provides a single source of truth.


That means in-store and online teams can work from the same information about products, inventory, orders and customers. For shoppers, it creates a more connected, seamless shopping experience. For example, a shopper can browse a dress on a brand’s mobile app, buy it online and later return it at any store location–while their purchase history and inventory automatically update everywhere in real time.
